nameStory: The name 'lavender' comes from the Latin 'lavare,' meaning 'to wash,' because Romans used this fragrant herb to scent their baths and laundry. Despite being called 'English lavender,' this Mediterranean native earned its English nickname simply because it grows so well in English gardens!
description: Common lavender is a small, bushy perennial herb that forms neat, rounded mounds about 2-3 feet tall and wide. It's famous for its intensely fragrant purple flower spikes that rise above silvery-gray, needle-like leaves. This Mediterranean native is widely grown in New England gardens for its wonderful scent, drought tolerance, and ability to attract bees and butterflies.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense spikes of tiny purple flowers cluster at the tips of long, square stems. The flowers have that unmistakable lavender fragrance that you can smell from several feet away, especially on warm days.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, gray-green leaves feel slightly fuzzy and release a strong, sweet scent when rubbed. They're arranged in opposite pairs along square stems - a telltale sign of the mint family.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a compact, woody-based shrub with multiple stems radiating from the center. The plant maintains its rounded, bushy shape even in winter, though it may look a bit scraggly.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square stems that feel firm and slightly woody at the base, becoming more herbaceous toward the tips. This square-stem feature is characteristic of all mint family plants.

habitat: In New England, you'll find common lavender almost exclusively in cultivated gardens, herb gardens, and landscaped areas. It thrives in well-drained, sunny spots and is often planted near walkways or patios where people can enjoy its fragrance. With only 3 recorded observations in New England, it's quite rare to find growing wild.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as fresh gray-green shoots from the woody base. Flower buds begin forming at stem tips by late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season from June through August, when the purple flower spikes are most fragrant and attract numerous bees and butterflies.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade but dried flower spikes often persist. Leaves remain aromatic and the plant keeps its bushy shape.
seasonality.winter: Woody stems and gray-green leaves persist, though the plant looks dormant. In harsh New England winters, it may die back partially or completely.

funFact: Lavender flowers actually get more fragrant when they're stressed by drought - the plant concentrates its essential oils as a survival mechanism, which is why the most aromatic lavender often comes from hot, dry Mediterranean hillsides!
confusionNotes: Russian sage has similar purple flowers and gray foliage, but its leaves are broader and more deeply cut, and it lacks lavender's distinctive sweet fragrance. Remember: if it doesn't smell like lavender soap, it's probably not lavender!
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'English lavender,' this plant is actually native to the Mediterranean and isn't truly native to England - or New England for that matter. The 'English' name simply refers to its popularity in English gardens, where the cooler, moister climate suits it better than some other lavender species.
compareHints: Common lavender is the only Lavandula species commonly grown in New England. Within the mint family, it's distinguished by its woody base and intensely fragrant, needle-like leaves. Other mint family members like bee balm or catnip have broader leaves and different flower structures, plus they lack lavender's distinctive sweet, floral scent.
